                                                              RISK IN RELATION TO THE FIRST ISSUE
 This being the first public issue of Equity Shares of our Company, there has been no formal market for Equity Shares. The face value of the Equity Shares is ₹10. The
 Floor Price and Cap Price determined by our Company in consultation with the Book Running Lead Manager (“BRLM”), and the Issue Price determined by our
 Company, in consultation with the BRLM, in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations and on the basis of the assessment of market demand for the Equity Shares
 by way of Book Building Process as stated in “Basis for the Issue Price” on page 128 should not be considered to be indicative of the market price of the Equity Shares
 after the Equity Shares are listed. No assurance can be given regarding an active and/or sustained trading in the Equity Shares nor regarding the price at which the Equity
 Shares will be traded after listing.

                                                     BOMBAY COATED AND SPECIAL STEELS LIMITED
                                               (Formerly Known as Bombay Coated and Special Steels Private Limited)
 Our Company was originally incorporated as ‘Bombay Coated and Special Steels Private Limited’, a private limited company under the provisions of Companies Act,
 2013 at Mumbai, Maharashtra, pursuant to a certificate of incorporation dated December 26, 2019, issued by Assistant Registrar of Companies, Central Registration
 Centre at Manesar, Haryana for and on behalf of the Jurisdictional Registrar of Companies, Mumbai at Maharashtra (“RoC”). Further, pursuant to Business Transfer
 Agreement dated January 29, 2021 (“BTA”) with Mr. Vijaykumar Himatrai Gupta, proprietor of M/s. Bombay Steels, Our Company acquired the running business of
 M/s. Bombay Steels. Thereafter, our Company was converted into a public limited company pursuant to a board resolution dated January 21, 2025 and a special
 resolution passed by our Shareholders dated January 22, 2025 and consequently, the name of our Company was changed to ‘Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited’.
 A fresh certificate of change of name, consequent upon conversion to a public limited company was issued by Registrar of Companies, Central Processing Centre,
 Manesar, Haryana on February 14, 2025. For further details on the changes in the name and registered office of our Company, see “History and Certain Corporate
 Matters” on page 281.

INITIAL PUBLIC OFFERING OF UP TO [●] EQUITY SHARES OF FACE VALUE OF ₹10 EACH (“EQUITY SHARES”) OF BOMBAY COATED AND
SPECIAL STEELS LIMITED (“OUR COMPANY” OR “ISSUER”) FOR CASH AT A PRICE OF ₹[●] PER EQUITY SHARE (INCLUDING A SHARE
PREMIUM OF ₹ [●] PER EQUITY SHARE) (“ISSUE PRICE”) AGGREGATING UP TO ₹1,830.57 MILLION (THE “ISSUE”). THE ISSUE COMPRISES A
FRESH ISSUE OF UP TO [●] EQUITY SHARES AGGREGATING UP TO ₹ [●] MILLION (THE “ISSUE”). THE ISSUE SHALL CONSTITUTE [●]% OF
THE POST-ISSUE PAID-UP EQUITY SHARE CAPITAL OF OUR COMPANY.

THE FACE VALUE OF EQUITY SHARES IS ₹10 EACH. THE ISSUE PRICE IS [●] TIMES THE VALUE OF THE EQUITY SHARES. THE PRICE BAND
AND THE MINIMUM BID LOT WILL BE DECIDED BY OUR COMPANY IN CONSULTATION WITH THE BOOK RUNNING LEAD MANAGER
(“BRLM”) AND WILL BE ADVERTISED IN FINANCIAL EXPRESS, AN ENGLISH NATIONAL DAILY NEWSPAPER, JANSATTA, A HINDI NATIONAL
DAILY NEWSPAPER AND NAVSHAKTI, A MARATHI NEWSPAPER, MARATHI BEING THE REGIONAL LANGUAGE OF MAHARASHTRA, WHERE
OUR REGISTERED OFFICE IS LOCATED, WITH WIDE CIRCULATION, AT LEAST TWO WORKING DAYS PRIOR TO THE BID/ISSUE OPENING
DATE AND SHALL BE MADE AVAILABLE TO BSE LIMITED AND NATIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE OF INDIA LIMITED (THE “STOCK
EXCHANGES”) FOR THE PURPOSE OF UPLOADING ON THEIR WEBSITES IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE BOARD
OF INDIA (ISSUE OF CAPITAL AND DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS) REGULATIONS, 2018, AS AMENDED (THE“SEBI ICDR REGULATIONS”).
In case of any revision in the Price Band, the Bid/Issue Period will be extended by at least three additional Working Days after such revision in the Price Band, subject to
the Bid/Issue Period not exceeding 10 Working Days. In cases of force majeure, banking strike or similar circumstances, our Company consulting with Book Running
Lead Manager, for reasons to be recorded in writing, extend the Bid/Issue Period for a minimum of three Working Days, subject to the Bid/Issue Period not exceeding 10
Working Days. Any revision in the Price Band and the revised Bid/Issue Period, if applicable, will be widely disseminated by notification to the Stock Exchanges, by
issuing a public notice, and by indicating the change on the website of the Book Running Lead Manager and at the terminals of the Syndicate Members and by intimation
to Designated Intermediaries and the Sponsor Bank, as applicable.
                 THE FACE VALUE OF THE EQUITY SHARES IS ₹10 EACH AND THE ISSUE PRICE IS [●] TIMES OF THE FACE VALUE
The Issue is being made in terms of Rule 19(2)(b) of the SCRR read with Regulation 31 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations. The Issue is being made through the Book Building
Process in accordance with Regulation 6(1) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations wherein not more than 50% of the Issue shall be available for allocation on a proportionate
basis to Qualified Institutional Buyers (“QIBs”) (the “QIB Portion”), provided that our Company, in consultation with the BRLM, may allocate up to 60% of the QIB
Portion to Anchor Investors and the basis of such allocation will be on a discretionary basis by our Company, in consultation with the BRLM, in accordance with the SEBI
ICDR Regulations (the “Anchor Investor Portion”), of which, 40% shall be reserved in the following manner, (i) 33.33% shall be available for allocation to domestic
Mutual Funds, and (ii) 6.67% shall be available for Life Insurance Companies and Pension Funds, subject to valid Bids being received from domestic Mutual Funds, Life
Insurance Companies and Pension Funds at or above the Anchor Investor Allocation Price. In the event of under-subscription in (ii) above, the allocation may be made to
domestic Mutual Funds. In the event of under-subscription, or non-allocation in the Anchor Investor Portion, the balance Equity Shares shall be added to the QIB Portion
(other than Anchor Investor Portion) (“Net QIB Portion”). Further, 5% of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a proportionate basis only to Mutual
Funds, subject to valid Bids being received at or above the Issue Price, and the remainder of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a proportionate basis
to all QIBs, including Mutual Funds, subject to valid Bids being received at or above the Issue Price. Further, not less than 15% of the Issue shall be available for allocation
to Non-Institutional Investors ( “Non-Institutional Portion”) of which one-third of the Non-Institutional Portion shall be available for allocation to Bidders with an
application size of more than ₹200,000 and up to ₹1,000,000 and two-thirds of the Non-Institutional Portion shall be available for allocation to Bidders with an application
size of more than ₹1,000,000 and under-subscription in either of these two sub-categories of Non-Institutional Portion may be allocated to Bidders in the other sub-category
of Non-Institutional Portion in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations, subject to valid Bids being received at or above the Issue Price. Further, not less than 35% of
the Issue shall be available for allocation to Retail Individual Investors (“Retail Portion”), in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations, subject to valid Bids being
received from them at or above the Issue Price. All Bidders (except Anchor Investors) shall mandatorily participate in this Issue only through the Application Supported
by Blocked Amount (“ASBA”) process and shall provide details of their respective bank account (including UPI ID (defined hereinafter) in case of UPI Bidders (defined
hereinafter)) in which the Bid Amount will be blocked by the Self Certified Syndicate Banks (“SCSBs”) or the Sponsor Bank(s), as the case may be. Anchor Investors are
not permitted to participate in the Anchor Investor Portion through the ASBA process. For details, see “Issue Procedure” beginning on page 502.

legislation made from time to time under that provision. Further, the Issue related terms used but not defined in this Red
Herring Prospectus shall have the meanings ascribed to such terms under the General Information Document. In case of
any inconsistency between the definitions given below and the definitions contained in the General Information Document
(as defined below), the definitions given below shall prevail.

The words and expressions used but not defined in this Red Herring Prospectus will (to the extent applicable) have the
same meaning as assigned to such terms under the SEBI ICDR Regulations, Companies Act 2013, the Securities and
Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, as amended (the “SEBI Act”), the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, as
amended (the “SCRA”), the Depositories Act, 1996, as amended (the “Depositories Act”) and the rules and regulations
made thereunder.

unless stated otherwise, all references to page numbers in this Red Herring Prospectus are to the page numbers of this Red
Herring Prospectus.

Financial Data

Our Company’s financial year commences on April 1st of the immediately preceding calendar year and ends on March 31st
of that particular calendar year. Accordingly, all references to a particular fiscal or financial year are to the 12-month period
commencing on April 1st of the immediately preceding calendar year and ending on March 31st of that particular calendar
year.

Unless the context requires otherwise, the financial information in this Red Herring Prospectus is derived from the restated
financial statements of our Company as at and for the three months period ended June 30, 2026, and financial years ended
March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024 comprising the restated statement of assets and liabilities as at June
30, 2026, March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024, the restated statements of profit and loss (including other
comprehensive income), the restated statements of changes in equity, the restated statements of cash flows, each for the
three months period ended June 30, 2026 and financial year ended March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024,
the summary statement of material accounting policies and other explanatory information, prepared as per the requirement
of Section 26 of Part I of Chapter III of the Companies Act, 2013, SEBI ICDR Regulations, and the Guidance Note on
‘Reports in Company Prospectuses (Revised 2019)’ issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (“ICAI”), as
amended. For further information, see “Restated Financial Information” on page 312.

There are significant differences between the Ind AS, the International Financial Reporting Standards issued by the
International Accounting Standard Board (the “IFRS”) and the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles in the United
States of America (the “U.S. GAAP”). Accordingly, the degree to which the financial information included in this Red
Herring Prospectus will provide meaningful information is entirely dependent on the reader’s level of familiarity with
Indian accounting practices. Any reliance by persons not familiar with accounting standards in India, the Ind AS, the
Companies Act 2013 and the SEBI ICDR Regulations, on the financial disclosures presented in this Red Herring Prospectus
should accordingly be limited. We have not attempted to quantify or identify the impact of the differences between the
financial data (prepared under Ind AS and IFRS/U.S. GAAP), nor have we provided a reconciliation thereof. We urge you
to consult your own advisors regarding such differences and their impact on our financial data included in this Red Herring
Prospectus. For details see, “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Conditions and Results of Operations”
and “Risk Factors – Significant differences exist between Ind AS and other accounting principles, such as IFRS and U.S.
GAAP), which may be material to investors’ assessments of our financial condition.” on pages 408 and 72, respectively.

Unless the context otherwise requires, any percentage, amounts, as set forth in “Risk Factors”, “Our Business” and
“Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Conditions and Results of Operations” on pages 30, 239 and 408,
respectively and elsewhere in this Red Herring Prospectus have been calculated on the basis of our Restated Financial
Information.

Prospective investors should consult their own professional advisers for an understanding of the differences between these
accounting principles and those with which they may be more familiar, and the impact on our financial data. The degree to
which the financial information included in this Red Herring Prospectus will provide meaningful information is entirely
dependent on the reader’s level of familiarity with Indian accounting policies and practices, Ind AS, the Companies Act
2013 and the SEBI ICDR Regulations. Any reliance by persons not familiar with these accounting principles and regulations
on our financial disclosures presented in this Red Herring Prospectus should accordingly be limited.

Non-Generally Accepted Accounting Principles Financial Measures

Certain non-generally accepted accounting principle (“Non-GAAP”) measures, such as Net Asset Value Per Equity Share,
EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, Total Cash and cash equivalents and Bank Balance (including fixed deposits and current
investments), Capital Employed, Adjusted Capital Employed, Return on Adjusted Capital Employed, Net Debt, Net Worth
and Total Revenue (“Non-GAAP Measures”) presented in this Red Herring Prospectus are a supplemental measure of our
performance and liquidity that are not required by, or presented in accordance with Ind AS or any other generally accepted
accounting. For details in relation to reconciliation of non-GAAP financial measures, see “Management’s Discussion and
Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations-Non-GAAP Financial Measures - Reconciliation of Non-GAAP
Measures” on page 454. Further, these Non-GAAP Measures are not a measurement of our financial performance or
liquidity under Ind AS or any other accepted accounting principles and should not be considered in isolation or construed
as an alternative to cash flows, profit/(loss) for the year/period or any other measure of financial performance or as an
indicator of our operating performance, liquidity, profitability or cash flows generated by operating, investing or financing
activities derived in accordance with Ind AS. In addition, the Non-GAAP Measures, as used by our Company and their
definition as set out herein, are not a standardised term, hence a direct comparison of similarly titled Non-GAAP Measures
between companies may not be possible. Other companies may calculate the Non-GAAP Measures differently from us,
limiting their usefulness as a comparative measure. Although the Non-GAAP Measures are not a measure of performance
calculated in accordance with applicable accounting standards, our Company’s management believes that they are useful
to an investor in evaluating us because they are widely used measures by securities analysts, investors and others to evaluate
a company’s operating performance. For further details, see “Risk Factors - Certain non-GAAP financial measures and
certain other statistical information relating to our operations and financial performance like Gross Profit, Gross Margin,
EBITDA, EBITDA Margin, PAT Margin, Return on Net Worth, Return on Capital Employed, Net Debt to Equity Ratio and
Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio have been included in this Red Herring Prospectus. These non-GAAP financial measures are
not measures of operating performance or liquidity defined by Ind AS and may not be comparable.” on page 69.

INTERNAL RISKS

1.   We are substantially dependent on a single supplier, JSW Steel Coated Products Limited and/or its holding
     Company (“JSWSCPL”), for the supply of steel coils, which constitute a key raw material for our operations. For
     the three months period ended June 30, 2026, and for the Fiscal 2026, Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2024, we sourced
     approximately 85.13%, 86.65%, 90.61% and 84.58%, respectively, of our total steel coil requirements from
     JSWSCPL. This high level of supplier concentration exposes us to significant risks, and any disruption in the supply
     of steel coils from JSWSCPL could materially and adversely affect our business, results of operations and financial
     condition.

                                                             30
We have been an authorised service partner of JSW Steel Coated Products Limited and/or its holding Company
(“JSWSCPL”) since 2021. For further details of our service partner arrangement, see “History and Certain Corporate
Matters – Other Material Agreements” on page 284. Under this arrangement, we procure steel coils from JSWSCPL and
undertake further value-added processing using high-precision engineering and machinery to manufacture processed steel
products, which are supplied to OEMs and ODMs in the home and commercial appliances and general engineering sectors.
These customers require processed steel products that meet specific technical and quality specifications, and our ability to
meet such requirements in a timely and cost-effective manner is closely linked to the continuity of supplies from JSWSCPL.

Any adverse change in our relationship with JSWSCPL, including reduction in supply volumes, changes in commercial
terms, modification, non-renewal or termination of our authorised service partner status, or operational disruptions at
JSWSCPL, could adversely affect our production schedules, increase our raw material costs, delay customer deliveries and
negatively impact our revenue and profitability.

Further, as an authorised service partner of JSWSCPL, we are subject to restrictions relating to the procurement of
galvanized plain coils/sheets and corrugated/profiled sheets, colour-coated coils/sheets and corrugated/profiled sheets, and
galvalume plain coils/sheets and corrugated/profiled sheets from suppliers other than JSWSCPL. These restrictions limit
our ability to diversify our supplier base for such steel products. If we were to source such products from alternative
suppliers, we may risk losing our authorised service partner status with JSWSCPL, which could significantly impair our
sourcing arrangements, customer relationships and business model. Although we have not experienced any disruption in
our relationship with JSWSCPL in the past, we cannot assure you that this relationship will continue on existing terms or
at all.

Our service partner arrangement with JSWSCPL does not grant us any exclusive territorial rights or sole service partner
status. JSWSCPL is entitled to appoint additional authorised service partners, including within our operating regions of
western, northern and southern India. The appointment of competing authorised service partners in our operating regions
could dilute our market position, reduce our bargaining power, intensify competition for customers and exert downward
pressure on pricing. In addition, JSWSCPL may expand its authorised service partner network or establish or expand its
own steel processing facilities, which could result in a reduction in volumes supplied to us and adversely affect our revenue
and profitability.

2. We have experienced certain discrepancies in our statutory filings with the Registrar of Companies (“RoC”) and other
non-compliances under the Companies Act, 2013 in the past. We cannot assure that regulatory authorities will not
initiate inquiries, proceedings or other actions against us in the future. Any such proceedings or actions, if initiated,
may result in the imposition of penalties, fines or other regulatory measures, which could adversely affect our business,
financial condition, results of operations and reputation.

Pursuant to a Business Transfer Agreement dated January 29, 2021 (“BTA”), our Company acquired the business of M/s.
Bombay Steels from Mr. Vijaykumar Himatrai Gupta, the proprietor of M/s. Bombay Steels and one of the Promoters of
our Company. In accordance with the terms of the BTA, the Company issued and allotted 24,50,000 equity shares to Mr.
Vijaykumar Himatrai Gupta in lieu of the balance consideration of ₹87.61 million, on a private placement basis. The
shareholders of the Company approved the said issue and allotment at their meeting held on February 24, 2021, and the
Board of Directors approved the allotment at its meeting held on March 9, 2021.

However, we inadvertently failed to file Form MGT-14 with the RoC in respect of the said private placement, as required
under the Companies Act, 2013. Further, while filing Form PAS-3 in respect of the said allotment, we erroneously selected
the mode of allotment as “Rights Issue” instead of “Issue of Shares for Consideration Other Than Cash.”

In order to rectify the aforesaid errors, we have filed a revised Form PAS-3 with the necessary corrections and have also
filed Form MGT-14 along with an adjudication application before the Registrar of Companies (“RoC”). In connection with
the adjudication proceedings, we received observations from the RoC dated November 12, 2025, to which we submitted
our response on December 5, 2025. Further, we filed a separate adjudication application on January 6, 2026 in respect of
the delay in filing Form MGT-14. The said adjudication application is currently pending before the RoC. In the event the
Company is aggrieved by the order passed by the Registrar of Companies (“RoC”), it shall file an appeal before the Regional
Director (“RD”) under Section 454 of the Companies Act, 2013, and, if necessary, pursue the matter further before the
appropriate appellate forums up to the court of last appeal. For further information, see “History and Certain Corporate
Matters – Details regarding material acquisitions or divestments of business/ undertakings, mergers, amalgamation, any
revaluation of assets, etc. in the last ten years” on page 283.

Further, pursuant to a communication dated March 11, 2026 received from the RoC, our Company filed an application with
the RoC on May 13, 2026 seeking the marking as defective/cancellation of the original Form PAS-3 bearing SRN
T08474322 dated March 12, 2021, while retaining the revised and corrected Form PAS-3 bearing SRN AB6835518 dated
September 15, 2025 on record. The said application is currently pending before the RoC.

as plant shutdowns, labor strikes, or other work stoppages, may adversely impact their production and, in turn, our sales.
However, we have not experienced any such instances in three months period ended June 30, 2026 and in Fiscals 2026,
2025 and 2024.We cannot assure that we will be able to maintain historical levels of business with our key customers or
reduce customer concentration in the future, which may adversely affect our business prospects and financial performance.

5.   The cost of raw materials and components consumed accounted for 87.60%, 90.51%, 92.97% and 89.14% of our
     total expenses for the three months period ended June 30, 2026 and for Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, respectively.
     Any volatility in prices, unavailability, or disruption in the timely and adequate supply of steel coils may materially
     and adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

Steel coils constitute our principal raw material, and the cost of our Processed Steel Products depends on our ability to
procure such raw materials at commercially acceptable prices and in sufficient quantities. The price and availability of steel
coils are subject to volatility and supply constraints arising from various external factors beyond our control, including
global and domestic demand-supply dynamics, logistics and processing costs, inflation, governmental regulations and
policies, overall economic conditions, production levels, market competition, duties and taxes, trade restrictions,
transportation costs and currency exchange rate fluctuations. The table below sets out the cost of raw materials and

Steel coils are traded commodities, and their prices are subject to significant fluctuations driven by macroeconomic
conditions and market dynamics. Any substantial increase in the prices of steel coils or disruption in their timely availability
could adversely impact our production schedules, operating margins and overall financial performance. While we seek to
mitigate these risks through multiple approved suppliers and industry practices such as price adjustment mechanisms with
OEM and ODM, we cannot assure that such measures will fully offset the impact of commodity price volatility or supply
constraints. Steel grade-wise price differentials are typically passed on by steel mills to OEMs through retrospective price
adjustments, which may not always align with our pricing cycles.

We generally maintain raw material inventory for approximately one to one and a half months during periods of seasonality
and for approximately two months under normal operating conditions. We procure steel coils based on tentative projections
provided by our customers. Steel coils are ordered from steel mills in alignment with such projections and within optimum
procurement timelines, subject to customer approvals and suppliers meeting our quality and volume requirements. As we
do not control our suppliers’ production schedules, we are exposed to risks of delay, shortfall or discontinuation in the
supply of raw materials. Any such disruption may result in delays in production, underutilisation of capacity or inability to
meet customer demand, and could also lead to unexpected increases in raw material costs. While we have not experienced
material disruptions in the supply of steel coils during the three months period ended June 30, 2026, and the last three
Fiscals that adversely impacted our business, we cannot assure you that such disruptions will not occur in the future. Any
prolonged or significant disruption could increase the cost of our raw materials and, consequently, the prices of our
processed steel products.

We have historically experienced fluctuations in steel coil procurement costs due to volatility in the steel market. We
generally follow a quarterly pricing model for both the procurement of steel coils and the sale of processed steel products,
which provides price stability for a fixed period and assists in cost control and margin management. However, increasing
global demand for steel, supply constraints or disruptions at suppliers’ facilities could impair their ability to supply steel
coils in a timely manner and at competitive prices. Further, while we may benefit from government safeguard duties or
regulatory measures that partially offset adverse pricing impacts arising from policy changes or trade-related developments,
such measures may not be sufficient to protect us from significant or sustained increases in steel prices. If we increase the
prices of our processed steel products to offset higher raw material costs, our customers may reduce their purchases, delay
orders or cancel contracts, which could materially and adversely affect demand for our products. If we are unable to pass
on cost increases to our customers or effectively manage fluctuations in steel prices, our business, results of operations,
financial condition and cash flows could be materially and adversely affected.

demand trends prevailing in these sectors. Demand for our processed steel products is dependent on the demand for end

8.   Our high debt-to-equity ratio could adversely affect our financial condition, results of operations, and business
     prospects.

As on June 30, 2026, our debt-to-equity ratio was 2 times. Our debt-to-equity ratio is relatively high, reflecting our
significant dependence on borrowings to fund our operations and growth initiatives. A high level of leverage exposes us to
several risks, including higher interest payment obligations, increased sensitivity to changes in interest rates, reduced
financial flexibility, and restrictions arising from covenants under our financing arrangements. Any inability to comply
with such covenants or to service our debt obligations in a timely manner could adversely affect our liquidity and financial
condition. Further, during periods of adverse economic conditions, industry downturns, or volatility in interest rates, our
cash flows may be insufficient to meet our debt servicing requirements. This may require us to refinance our borrowings
on unfavourable terms or limit our ability to raise additional debt or equity financing. Any deterioration in our credit profile
could result in higher borrowing costs, more restrictive terms, or limited access to capital markets.

Accordingly, our high debt-to-equity ratio may materially and adversely affect our financial condition, results of operations,
cash flows, and ability to pursue our growth strategy. The following table sets forth details of our debt-to-equity ratio for
the three months period ended June 30, 2026 and for the financial years ended March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025, and March
31, 2024.

9.   Under-utilisation of our manufacturing capacities over extended periods, or significant under-utilisation in the
     short term, could increase our cost of production and operating costs, which could adversely affect our operating
     leverage, margins and financial performance.

Our capacity utilisation levels are influenced by several factors, including the level and timing of customer orders, demand
for our processed steel products, availability of raw materials, continuity of operations at our manufacturing facilities, and
prevailing industry and market conditions. In the event of a decline in demand for our processed steel products, prolonged
disruptions at our manufacturing facilities, delays in customer offtake, or our inability to procure adequate quantities of raw
materials, our capacity utilisation may decline and we may not be able to achieve optimal utilisation of our existing or
future manufacturing facilities.

We operate slitting, cut-to-length, shearing and embossing lines across our manufacturing facilities. These steel processing
lines are capital-intensive and are designed to operate efficiently at higher throughput levels. Under-utilisation of our
processing capacities limits our ability to absorb fixed costs over larger production volumes, which could adversely affect
our operating leverage and margins. Factors such as fluctuations in customer demand for our processed steel products,
seasonality, uneven order inflows across facilities, or delays in execution or cancellation of customer orders may result in
sub-optimal utilisation of our processing infrastructure.

Sustained under-utilisation of capacity may also lead to lower asset turnover, delayed returns on capital investments and
inefficiencies in working capital management. In addition, prolonged or significant short-term under-utilisation may limit
our ability to benefit from economies of scale, increase per-unit production costs and reduce the efficiency of our operations.
Any such developments could materially and adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition, cash
flows and growth prospects. The table below sets out our overall capacity utilisation for the periods indicated.

facilities. Any unscheduled or prolonged disruption at one or more of our facilities could adversely affect our ability to
manufacture products, meet customer demand in a timely manner and maintain operational efficiency. Such disruptions
could also have a disproportionate impact on our revenue, as reflected in the regional contribution of our manufacturing
facilities for the three months period ended June 30, 2026 and for the Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024.

Our manufacturing operations are exposed to various operational and location-specific risks, including fire, unexpected
mechanical failure of equipment, industrial accidents, disruptions in electrical power, earthquakes and other natural
disasters, adverse weather conditions, pandemics, labour availability and industrial relations issues, and significant social,
political or economic disturbances in the regions where our facilities are located. The occurrence of any such events could
result in loss of production, delays in customer deliveries, increased repair and maintenance costs, higher operating expenses
and potential loss of customers. In addition, our manufacturing facilities are subject to region-specific regulatory
frameworks and require various approvals, licenses, permits and consents from central, state and local authorities. If we are
found to be in contravention of any conditions attached to such regulatory approvals, or if such approvals are suspended,
cancelled or not renewed in a timely manner, we may be required to suspend or restrict operations at the affected facilities
until such matters are resolved.

While we have not experienced any material disruption at our manufacturing facilities during the three months period ended
June 30, 2026 and for the last three Fiscals, there can be no assurance that such disruptions will not occur in the future or
that their impact, if any, will not be material. Any disruption to the operations of our manufacturing facilities, whether due
to operational failures, regulatory actions or regional factors, could materially and adversely affect our business, financial
condition and results of operations.

12. We do not have long-term purchase commitments from our customers, and any reduction or cancellation of orders
    could adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

We do not have agreements with our customers that obligate them to purchase or place orders with us on a long-term basis.
If our customers choose not to source their requirements from us, or reduce or discontinue their purchases, it could have a
material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

Our sales are primarily based on customer purchase orders and forecasts, which is common in the steel processing industry.
These purchase orders generally set out the commercial terms of sale but do not bind customers to purchase any specific
steel processing products, specifications, volumes, or for any defined duration. Such purchase orders may be terminated by


                                                                44
customers, with or without cause, and without compensation. These arrangements do not always provide for minimum
purchase commitments. Consequently, customers may reduce, delay, or cancel their orders at any time, which could
adversely affect our business and results of operations.

If we fail to fulfil purchase orders or contractual obligations in a timely manner, particularly in relation to OEM and ODM
customers, or fail to fulfil them at all, some of our customers may be entitled to terminate the relevant order or contract
without any further liability or obligation towards us. While we have not experienced any product recalls due to
manufacturing quality issues, component defects, rejection of product batches, product discontinuations or termination of
customer relationships during the three months period ended June 30, 2026 and the last three Fiscals, there can be no
assurance that such events will not occur in the future. The following table indicates total number of customers for the
reporting period:

We have long-standing relationships with many of our customers, with several having been associated with us since the
commencement of our operations. For the three-month period ended June 30, 2026, and for Fiscal 2026, Fiscal 2025 and
Fiscal 2024, approximately 98.05%, 96.08%, 93.76% and 87.88%, respectively, of our restated revenue from operations
was derived from existing customers. As of June 30, 2026, our relationships with several of our top 10 customers ranged
from one and a half years to over three years. However, there can be no assurance that such customers will continue to
place orders with us at similar levels in the future. While there have been no such material instances of loss of long-standing
customers as at and for the three months period ended June 30, 2026 and during the Fiscals 2026, 2025 or 2024, we cannot
assure you that such incidents will not occur in future.

Additionally, although our contracts generally do not provide for exclusivity, we have not experienced any instances during
the three months period ended June 30, 2026, and the last three Fiscals of losing business to competitors due to such non-
exclusivity. However, we cannot assure you that increased competition or customers sourcing similar products from
competitors will not adversely affect our business, results of operations and financial condition in the future.

13. Our success depends upon knowledge and experience of our Directors, Key Managerial Personnel, Senior
    Management and other key employees as well as our ability to attract and retain personnel with technical expertise.
    In the three months period ended June 30, 2026, Fiscal 2026, Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2024, our Company’s attrition
    rate for permanent employees was 4.30%, 26.10%, 32.13% and 44.21%, respectively. The loss of or our inability to
    attract or retain such persons could adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and
    cash flows.

Our operations and future growth are dependent on our ability to attract, retain and motivate qualified and skilled personnel,
including our Directors, Key Managerial Personnel, Senior Management and other key employees. We currently have
adequate qualified personnel, given the demand for skilled professionals in our industry, we may not be able to continuously
attract or retain such personnel, including due to attrition, or retain them on acceptable terms. The loss of the services of
such personnel, or an increase in attrition levels, may adversely affect our operations, execution capabilities and business
continuity. Competition for skilled and experienced personnel in our industry is intense, and our competitors may offer
compensation and benefit structures that are more attractive than ours. As a result, we may be required to increase employee
compensation and other incentives at a faster rate than in the past to remain competitive. There can be no assurance that we
will be successful in attracting and retaining a sufficient number of qualified personnel to support our existing operations
and expansion plans. Any failure to do so could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations,
financial condition and cash flows.

14. Our funding requirements and proposed deployment of the Net Proceeds of the Issue have not been appraised by
    any bank or financial institution, and any delays, cost overruns or changes in the proposed utilisation may adversely
    affect our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.

We intend to utilise the Net Proceeds of the Issue for a) repayment and/or pre-payment, in full or in part, of certain
borrowings availed by our Company; b) financing the cost towards acquisition of capital equipment under existing lease
arrangements with Siemens Financial Services Private Limited; and c) general corporate purposes, as described in the

                                                                  46
section titled “Objects of the Issue” on page 117. The proposed utilisation of the Net Proceeds has not been appraised by
any bank, financial institution or any other independent external agency. The proposed deployment of the Net Proceeds is
based on our current business plans, management estimates, prevailing market conditions and commercial considerations
and, in relation to the acquisition of capital equipment under existing lease arrangements with Siemens Financial Services
Private Limited, the foreclosure letter received from Siemens Financial Services Private Limited and the fair market value
report for plant and machinery issued by an IBBI-registered valuer. However, these estimates and assumptions are subject
to change due to factors beyond our control, including variations in actual costs incurred, vendor quotations, price
fluctuations, demand conditions and other unforeseen circumstances, and there can be no assurance that the actual
expenditure will not differ from our estimates. Any increase in costs or deviation from assumptions may require us to fund
such excess expenditure through internal accruals or additional borrowings, which may not be available on commercially
acceptable terms or at all, and could adversely affect our revenues, earnings, implementation timelines, results of operations,
financial condition and cash flows.

Further, the deployment of the Net Proceeds towards the Objects of the Issue is at the discretion of our management and
subject to approval by our Board or the IPO Committee. The exact amount to be utilised for each object will depend on our
business requirements, economic conditions, competitive landscape, regulatory environment and other factors affecting our
operations, financial condition and access to capital. Any delay in implementation, cost overruns or failure to achieve the
intended objectives may adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows. Pending
utilisation of the Net Proceeds, we intend to temporarily deposit the Net Proceeds in deposits with one or more scheduled
commercial banks included in the Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, as approved by our Board or
IPO Committee. Although we propose to appoint a monitoring agency to monitor utilisation of the Gross Proceeds,
prospective investors will be required to rely on the judgment of our management regarding the deployment of the Net
Proceeds.

Various risks and uncertainties, including those described in this “Risk Factors” section, may limit or delay our ability to
utilise the Net Proceeds to achieve our growth objectives. Accordingly, the use of the Net Proceeds may not result in actual
growth, increased profitability or enhancement in shareholder value, and investors may lose part or all of their investment.

15. Our business requires significant working capital, and any inability to arrange or maintain adequate working
    capital may adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

Our business requires significant amounts of working capital, including for the procurement of raw materials and
components and for the processing and manufacture of our processed steel products, prior to receiving payments from our
customers. Our working capital requirements may increase if our contractual or sales arrangements do not provide for
advance payments or where payments are required to be made only upon delivery of the final products. Further, our working
capital requirements may also increase if we undertake a higher volume of orders as a result of the growth of our business.

16. Our business is capital intensive, and our significant capital expenditure requirements may constrain our ability to
    expand into new product lines or business segments and adversely affect our business, results of operations,
    financial condition and cash flows.

Our business is capital intensive and requires substantial capital expenditure for the establishment, expansion and
maintenance of our steel processing facilities, including investments in plant and machinery, processing lines and related
infrastructure. Any failure to adequately fund our capital expenditure requirements may adversely affect our operations and
growth prospects. We have incurred significant capital expenditure during the last three Fiscals, and the three month period
ended June 30, 2026, details of which are set out in the table below.

Expanding our customer base within the same industry segment is subject to several structural and operational constraints.
Many prospective customers maintain long-standing supply arrangements and technical alignments with their existing steel
processors and alternate vendors, which makes it difficult for new suppliers to displace incumbent vendors. In addition,
certain customers require specific steel grades or product types that may not be available with us or that we may not be able
to procure from our suppliers on commercially acceptable terms. Further, our existing processing capabilities may not
always meet the specialized technical requirements of such customers. These factors create high entry barriers in the steel
processing ecosystem and may limit our ability to successfully onboard new customers.

Similarly, our ability to diversify into new product lines, business segments, or markets is subject to significant risks arising
from the low-margin and highly competitive nature of the steel processing sector, which may limit our ability to achieve
and sustain profitability in such segments. Our expansion efforts may require us to secure reliable supply arrangements for
specialized steel grades, obtain customer acceptance, and adapt our operational capabilities to meet stringent quality,
pricing, and delivery requirements, any of which may be time-consuming, uncertain, or unsuccessful. Further, such
initiatives may necessitate additional working capital to support inventory, manpower, and operational enhancements,
which may not be available on commercially acceptable terms or at all. Any inability to successfully diversify or to generate
expected returns from such initiatives could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, and
cash flows.

To fund our capital expenditure requirements, we may rely on a combination of internal accruals, debt financing and the
issuance of equity shares. Our internally generated funds may not be sufficient to meet our future capital expenditure
requirements, which could necessitate raising additional capital. If we incur additional indebtedness, our interest costs and
debt servicing obligations will increase, which could adversely affect our profitability, cash flows and financial condition.
Further, there can be no assurance that additional financing will be available to us in a timely manner or on commercially
acceptable terms, or at all. If we are unable to obtain adequate financing when required, we may be required to defer, scale
down or modify our capital expenditure and growth plans, which could adversely affect our business, results of operations,


                                                               48
financial condition and cash flows. In addition, any equity financing may result in dilution of the shareholding of our
existing shareholders.

17. As of August 31, 2026, our Company has significant outstanding borrowings of ₹3,024.28 million and is subject to
    restrictive covenants under our financing arrangements, which may limit our operational and financial flexibility
    and adversely affect our business and liquidity.

As of August 31, 2026, we had total outstanding borrowings of ₹ 3,024.28 million. Certain of our financing arrangements
contain restrictive covenants that require us to obtain prior consent or provide intimation to the respective lenders before
undertaking specified actions and transactions. These covenants vary depending on the lender and the terms negotiated
under each financing agreement. Such actions include, among others, changes to our capital structure or shareholding,
amendments to our memorandum or articles of association, changes in the composition of our Board, undertaking mergers,
de-mergers, consolidations, reorganisations, schemes of arrangement or compromise with creditors or shareholders,
changes in the general nature of our business, or undertaking expansion or investments in other entities. While we have
obtained all necessary consents required for the purposes of this Issue, any failure to comply with such covenants or to
obtain requisite approvals in the future could restrict or delay corporate actions or business initiatives and may have an
adverse effect on our operations. In addition, certain of our secured borrowing facilities permit lenders to recall the
outstanding amounts on demand, including upon the occurrence of events that may be beyond our control. There can be no
assurance that we will be able to obtain waivers or extensions from our lenders or prevent such recalls, which could
adversely affect our operations, liquidity and cash flows.

Non-compliance with the covenants under our financing arrangements or failure to obtain required consents or waivers
may result in acceleration of repayment obligations or trigger cross-default provisions. In such an event, we may be required
to utilise a significant portion of our cash flows to service such obligations, thereby reducing funds available for working
capital and other general corporate purposes. Although there have been no instances of loan recall, invocation of promoter
guarantees, material covenant breaches, events of default, repayment defaults, rescheduling of loans, acceleration of
borrowings or triggering of cross-default provisions during the three months period ended June 30, 2026 and last three
Fiscals, there can be no assurance that such events will not occur in the future.

18. Any delay by our customers in taking delivery of our Processed Steel Products, due to internal or external factors,
    may result in an increase in our inventory levels and a corresponding delay in receipt of payments. Such delays may
    also constrain our ability to process further orders, which could adversely affect our business, results of operations
    and financial performance.

Effective inventory management is critical to meeting customer demand and maintaining cost-efficient operations. As part
of our steel processing activities, we also perform logistics- and inventory-related functions for certain customers by holding
inventory and offering just-in-time delivery to ensure timely and efficient supply of Processed Steel Products. However,
our inventory management processes may be disrupted due to factors such as logistical challenges or natural disasters,
which could lead to delays in delivery schedules, inaccuracies in inventory levels and increased operational costs. Any
inability to effectively manage our inventory could materially impair our growth and profitability.

We generally plan our production and supply schedules based on demand guidance received from a majority of our
customers. However, not all customers provide regular or detailed forecasts, and the frequency and quality of such guidance

                                                              49
may vary depending on the customer relationship. In cases where forecasts are not provided, we rely on historical demand
patterns to plan procurement and production schedules, which may result in inventory-related challenges. Any delay by
customers in accepting delivery of Processed Steel Products may further exacerbate inventory accumulation, delay cash
inflows and adversely impact our ability to process additional orders, which could have a material adverse effect on our
business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

23. Obsolescence, breakdown, or failure to maintain our equipment could adversely affect our business, financial
    condition, cash flows, and results of operations.

Our manufacturing operations are dependent on the seamless and continuous functioning of our machinery and equipment.
Over time, such equipment may become obsolete due to technological advancements, changes in industry standards, or
normal wear and tear. Any failure to timely upgrade, replace, or modernize our equipment, or to adopt advanced
technologies, may result in reduced operational efficiency, increased operating costs, and deterioration in product quality.

In order to ensure that our processed steel products comply with applicable industry standards and customer specifications,
we have installed various testing machines and equipment at our facilities, including the following:




                                                             57
 Type       of       testing    Method and purpose
 equipment/machine
 Vickers hardness tester        Measures the hardness of steel by pressing a diamond-shaped indenter into the surface and
                                assessing the size of the resulting impression, indicating the material’s strength and
                                suitability for intended use.
 Rockwell hardness tester       Determines steel hardness by measuring the depth of penetration of a small indenter under
                                load, indicating the strength and hardness of the material.
 Cross hatch tester             Evaluates the adhesion of coatings or paint on steel by cutting a grid pattern and assessing
                                whether the coating adheres or peels off.
 Pencil hardness tester         Measures the surface hardness and scratch resistance of coatings applied on steel using
                                pencils of varying hardness.
 Cupping test machine           Assesses the formability and ductility of metal sheets by pressing a ball-shaped tool into
                                the sheet until cracking occurs.
 Impact test machine            Tests the toughness of steel by measuring the amount of energy absorbed when the
                                material is struck by a pendulum, indicating resistance to sudden impact.
 T-bend tester                  Evaluates the flexibility and crack resistance of coatings when steel sheets are bent around
                                a specified radius.
 Methyl    Ethyl   Ketone       Tests the chemical resistance and durability of coatings by repeatedly rubbing a cloth
 (MEK) testing machine          soaked in MEK until signs of coating degradation appear.

Despite the installation of such machinery and testing equipment, inadequate maintenance, delayed repairs, obsolescence,
or unforeseen breakdowns may result in unplanned production stoppages, increased repair or replacement costs, and delays
in fulfilling customer orders. Such disruptions could adversely affect our production schedules, customer relationships, and
overall operational efficiency. While we have not experienced any such event during the three-months period ended June
30, 2026 and in the last three Fiscals March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024.

Further, prolonged downtime or recurring equipment failures may divert management attention, strain operational
resources, and adversely impact our reputation. Individually or collectively, any of the foregoing risks could have a material
adverse effect on our business, cash flows, financial condition, and results of operations.

24. Information relating to the installed capacity, utilised capacity and capacity utilisation of our manufacturing
    facilities included in this Red Herring Prospectus is based on assumptions and estimates, and actual production
    and capacity utilisation may vary.

The information relating to the installed capacity, utilised capacity, and percentage of capacity utilisation of our steel
processing products disclosed in this Red Herring Prospectus is based on certain assumptions and estimates made by our
management, which have been considered by the independent chartered engineer, M/s. S. Ganesan (Registration No.
M100949/9), while determining such capacity. These assumptions include standard industry practices for capacity
determination and the capacity of ancillary equipment installed at our manufacturing facilities. The determination of
installed capacity and the corresponding computation of capacity utilisation are, inter alia, based on the assumptions of 365
working days in a year and operations being carried out in two shifts per day of 12 hours each. However, out of our four
manufacturing facilities, one facility, namely the Sri City facility in Andhra Pradesh, currently operates in a single shift of
approximately 8 to 12 hours per day. Consequently, the actual utilised capacity and the percentage of capacity utilisation
at such facility may differ from the capacity levels computed based on the aforesaid assumptions.

Accordingly, actual production levels, utilised capacity and capacity utilisation across our manufacturing facilities may
vary materially from the installed capacity, utilised capacity and capacity utilisation figures disclosed in this Red Herring
Prospectus. Investors should not place undue reliance on such capacity information or historical capacity utilisation data.
For further details, see “Our Business – Installed Capacity and Capacity Utilization” on page 261.

we are unable to pass on such increase to our customers, could adversely affect our cost of production and profitability.
Interruptions or disruptions in the supply of electricity may result in production shutdowns, increased costs associated with
restarting operations and loss of production in progress. Further, any sustained increase in power tariffs or frequent supply
interruptions may require us to install captive power generation capacity, resulting in incremental capital expenditure, which
could adversely impact our results of operations. If energy costs were to rise, or if electricity supplies or supply
arrangements were disrupted, our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows may be adversely
affected. While there has been no instance of interruption in electricity supply or any operational shutdown during the three
months period ended June 30, 2026 and in the last three Fiscals, there can be no assurance that such instances will not arise
in the future.

28. We are required to comply with precise technical specifications, quality standards and performance requirements
    prescribed by our customers. Any failure to meet such specifications or standards could result in cancellation of
    orders, rejection or return of our Processed Steel Products, loss of customers and damage to our reputation, which

We operate as a multi-location steel processing centre catering to customised steel requirements of customers in the Home
& Commercial Appliances sector and the General Engineering sector. Our customers, including leading OEMs and ODMs
such as Haier Appliances India Private Limited, IFB Refrigeration Limited, Dixon Electro Manufacturing Private Limited,
Amber Enterprises India Limited, Western Refrigeration Private Limited, PG Technoplast Private Limited, EPack Durable

aesthetic specifications of the Processed Steel Products. Adherence to these parameters is critical to our operations. Any

defects in the Steel Coils processed by us, failure to meet customer specifications or deviations from prescribed quality
standards may result in order cancellations, product rejections or returns. Such events could require us to replace rejected

relationships and financial performance. Repeated quality lapses may further result in loss of customers and negatively
affect our business prospects.

Certain customers conduct vendor qualification reviews, technical audits and quality inspections, either directly or through

of defective products, expose us to liquidated damages, invocation of performance bank guarantees, security deposits,
indemnity or liability claims, or result in product recalls. Such events could have a material adverse effect on our business,
reputation, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

Further, supply of products contrary to specifications may expose us to litigation initiated by customers. In addition, we
may be subject to warranty or product liability claims by customers or third parties in the event that the use of our products
results in personal injury or property damage. Although we maintain quality control processes and have not faced any such

32. We face competition from domestic steel processing companies as well as steel producers that operate steel
    processing units, and any inability on our part to compete effectively may have a material adverse effect on our
    business, results of operations and financial condition.

We operate in a highly competitive environment in India and overseas. Competition in our industry is based on several
factors, including product quality and reliability, breadth of processed steel product offerings, innovation and technology,
manufacturing capabilities, scope and quality of service, pricing and brand recognition. We face competition from both
domestic and global players for retaining existing customers as well as for acquiring new business. Some of our competitors
may have certain advantages over us, including greater financial, technical and/or marketing resources, which may enable
them to finance acquisitions, fund international expansion, respond more quickly to technological changes, or operate across
more diversified geographies and product portfolios. Our peers include BMW Industries Limited, Manaksia Coated Metals
& Industries Limited and Shiv Aum Steels Limited (Source: CareEdge Report). For further information on financial
benchmarking, see “Industry Overview – Peer Comparison” on page 143.

Increased competition may result in pricing pressure, reduced margins and a loss of market share, any of which could
adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows. Certain competitors may also be
able to manufacture similar or substitute products at lower costs than us, which may require us to reduce prices in order to
remain competitive. Such pricing pressures could adversely impact our profitability and operating margins. Further,
manufacturers that do not currently compete with us may expand their product offerings to include products that directly
compete with ours. In addition, changes in the product focus of larger manufacturers, particularly those that have existing
relationships with our customers, could result in a reduction or complete loss of business from such customers. Any inability
to effectively compete in our industry could materially adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of
operations and cash flows.

Our business is subject to continuous technological advancements affecting steel processing methods, manufacturing

The regulatory and policy environment in which we operate are evolving and are subject to change. The Government of

                                                             72
We are subject to laws and government regulations, including in relation to safety, health, environmental protection and
labour. These laws and regulations impose controls on air and water discharge, employee exposure to hazardous substances
and other aspects of our steel processing operations. Further, laws and regulations may limit the amount of hazardous and
pollutant discharge that our manufacturing facilities may release into the air and water. The discharge of materials that
hazardous into the air, soil or water beyond these limits may cause us to be liable to regulatory bodies or third parties. Any
of the foregoing could subject us to litigation, which could lower our profits in the event we were found liable and could
also adversely affect our reputation. Additionally, the government or the relevant regulatory bodies may require us to shut
down our manufacturing facilities, which in turn could lead to product shortages that delay or prevent us from fulfilling our
obligations to customers.

For instance, the GoI has recently introduced the Code on Social Security, 2020 (“Social Security Code”); the Occupational
Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020; the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 and the Code on Wages, 2019,
which consolidate, subsume and replace numerous existing central labor legislations (collectively, the “Labour Codes”)
which have come into force pursuant to notification by the Ministry of Labour and Employment dated November 21, 2025.
While the draft rules for implementation under these codes have been recently notified, we have not yet fully assessed the
impact that these or similar laws might have on our business operations, which could potentially restrict our ability to grow
our business in the future and increase our expenses. For instance, the Social Security Code provides that where an employee
receives more than half (or such other percentage as may be notified by the Central Government) of their total remuneration
in the form of allowances and other amounts that are not included within the definition of wages under the Social Security
Code, the excess amount received shall be deemed as remuneration and accordingly be added to wages for the purposes of
the Social Security Code. Additionally, the Code on Wages, 2019, prescribes that if payments made by an employer towards
certain employment benefits (including gratuity and house rent allowance) exceed half (or such other percentage as may be
notified by the Central Government) of the total remuneration, the excess amount shall be deemed remuneration and
accordingly be added to wages. The enforcement of these laws could lead to higher employee and labor costs, which in turn
could have a detrimental effect on our results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

Uncertainty in the applicability, interpretation or implementation of any amendment to, or change in, governing law,
regulation or policy in the jurisdictions in which we operate, including by reason of an absence, or a limited body, of
administrative or judicial precedent may be time consuming as well as costly for us to resolve and may impact the viability
of our current business or restrict our ability to grow our business in the future. We may incur increased costs and other
burdens relating to compliance with such new requirements, which may also require significant management time and other
resources, and any failure to comply may adversely affect our business, results of operations, cash flows, financial condition
and prospects. Further, pursuant to the Finance (No.2) Act of 2024 and Finance Act, 2025, notified on August 16, 2024 and
March 29, 2025, respectively, the Government of India has introduced new income tax slabs, an increase in standard
deduction and an increase in the deduction available in respect of private sector employer’s contribution to National Pension
Scheme from 10% to 14% of the salary of the concerned employees. There is no certainty on the impact of the full union
budget on tax laws or other regulations, on our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows, or on the
industry in which we operate.

    affect our business.

The Competition Act, 2002, of India, as amended (“Competition Act”), regulates practices having an appreciable adverse
effect on competition (“AAEC”) in the relevant market in India. Under the Competition Act, any formal or informal
arrangement, understanding or action in concert, which causes or is likely to cause an AAEC is considered void and may
result in the imposition of substantial penalties. Further, any agreement among competitors which directly or indirectly
involves the determination of purchase or sale prices, limits or controls production, supply, markets, technical development,
investment or the provision of services or shares the market or source of production or provision of services in any manner,
including by way of allocation of geographical area or number of consumers in the relevant market or directly or indirectly
results in bid-rigging or collusive bidding is presumed to have an AAEC and is considered void. The Competition Act also
prohibits abuse of a dominant position by any enterprise. If it is proved that the contravention committed by a company
took place with the consent or connivance or is attributable to any neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary
or other officer of such company, that person shall be also guilty of the contravention and may be punished.

Further, the CCI has extra-territorial powers and can investigate any agreements, abusive conduct or combination occurring
outside India if such agreement, conduct or combination has an AAEC in India. However, the impact of the provisions of
the Competition Act on the agreements entered into by us cannot be predicted with certainty at this stage. In the event we
pursue an acquisition in the future, we may be affected, directly or indirectly, by the application or interpretation of any
provision of the Competition Act, or any enforcement proceedings initiated by the CCI, or any adverse publicity that may
be generated due to scrutiny or prosecution by the CCI or if any prohibition or substantial penalties are levied under the
Competition Act, it would adversely affect our business, results of operations, cash flows and prospects. The manner in
which the Competition Act and the CCI affect the business environment in India may also adversely affect our business,
results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 (“Competition Amendment Act”) was notified on April 11, 2023, which
amends the Competition Act and give the CCI additional powers to prevent practices that harm competition and the interests
of consumers. The Competition Amendment Act, inter alia, modifies the scope of certain factors used to determine AAEC,
reduces the overall time limit for the assessment of combinations by the CCI from 210 days to 150 days and empowers the
CCI to impose penalties based on the global turnover of entities, for anticompetitive agreements and abuse of dominant
position. We have not experienced any instances wherein we were subject to any penalty or received any notice from the
CCI in the last three Fiscals, we cannot assure you such instances will not arise in the future.

61. Financial and political instability in other countries may cause increased volatility in Indian financial markets.

The Indian market and the Indian economy are influenced by economic and market conditions in other countries, including
conditions in the United States of America, Europe and certain emerging economies in Asia. In particular, the ongoing
military conflicts between India and Pakistan, Russia and Ukraine and, Iran, Israel and Palestine could result in increased
volatility in, or damage to, the worldwide financial markets and economy. Increased economic volatility and trade
restrictions could result in increased volatility in the markets for certain securities and commodities and may cause inflation.
Any other global economic developments or the perception that any of them could occur may continue to have an adverse
effect on global economic conditions and the stability of global financial markets, and may significantly reduce global
market liquidity and restrict the ability of key market participants to operate in certain financial markets. Further, any
worldwide financial instability including possibility of default in the US debt market may cause increased volatility in the
Indian financial markets and, directly or indirectly, adversely affect the Indian economy and financial sector and us.
Although economic conditions are different in each country, investors’ reactions to developments in one country can have
adverse effects on the securities of companies in other countries, including India. A loss of investor confidence in the
financial systems of other emerging markets may cause increased volatility in Indian financial markets and, indirectly, in
the Indian economy in general. Concerns related to a trade war between large economies may lead to increased risk aversion
and volatility in global capital markets and consequently have an impact on the Indian economy.

More recently, in early 2025, the United States of America imposed tariffs across a range of countries and products. In
addition, President of the United States of America has directed various federal agencies to further evaluate key aspects of
U.S. trade policy, and there has been ongoing discussion and commentary regarding potential significant changes to U.S.
trade policies and treaties. The timing, amount and impact of such measures (including any retaliatory measures) cannot be

                                                              74
predicted but could result in lower economic growth. Market reactions to the uncertainty of such measures could further
depress economic activity until more clarity about trade conditions and tariffs is achieved. Such adverse economic or
financial conditions could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash
flows.

In addition, China is one of India’s major trading partners and there are rising concerns of a possible slowdown in the
Chinese economy as well as a strained relationship with India, which could have an adverse impact on the trade relations
between the two countries. In response to such developments, legislators and financial regulators in the United States of
America and other jurisdictions, including India, implemented a number of policy measures designed to add stability to the
financial markets. Further, the imposition of tariffs by the US government under its “Fair and Reciprocal Plan” may
impact Indian businesses, especially those with a substantial export presence in the US market. This policy has resulted in
the imposition of tariffs across a diverse range of sectors, including steel, aluminium, pharmaceuticals, textiles, and
electronics. As a results, Indian exporters may encounter heightened costs and uncertainties, potentially constraining their
market competitiveness and profitability. These developments, or the perception that any of them could occur, have had
and may continue to have an adverse effect on global economic conditions and the stability of global financial markets, and
may significantly reduce global market liquidity, restrict the ability of key market participants to operate in certain financial
markets or restrict our access to capital. However, the overall long-term effect of these and other legislative and regulatory
efforts on the global financial markets is uncertain, and they may not have the intended stabilising effects.

62. The Indian tax regime has undergone substantial changes which could adversely affect our business and the trading
    price of the Equity Shares.

Any change in Indian tax laws could have an effect on our operations. The Government of India has implemented two
major reforms in Indian tax laws, namely the Goods and Services Tax (“GST”), and provisions relating to general anti-
avoidance rules (“GAAR”). The indirect tax regime in India has undergone a complete overhaul. The indirect taxes on
goods and services, such as central excise duty, service tax, central sales tax, state value added tax, surcharge and excise
have been replaced by GST with effect from July 1, 2017. Further, on September 3, 2025, the 56th GST Council approved
a significant rate rationalisation package consolidating existing slabs into 5% and 18% (with 40% for luxury/sin goods) and
reducing GST on individual health and life insurance premiums from 18% to 0%, effective September 22, 2025. The GST
regime continues to be subject to amendments and its interpretation by the relevant regulatory authorities is constantly
evolving. GAAR became effective from April 1, 2017. The tax consequences of the GAAR provisions being applied to an
arrangement may result in, among others, a denial of tax benefit to us and our business. In the absence of any substantial
precedents on the subject, the application of these provisions is subjective. If the GAAR provisions are made applicable to
us, it may have an adverse tax impact on us. Further, if the tax costs associated with certain of our transactions are greater
than anticipated because of a particular tax risk materializing on account of new tax regulations and policies, it could affect
our profitability from such transactions.

Earlier, distribution of dividends by a domestic company was subject to Dividend Distribution Tax (“DDT”), in the hands
of the company at an effective rate of 20.56% (inclusive of applicable surcharge and cess). Such dividends were generally
exempt from tax in the hands of the shareholders. However, the GoI has amended the Income-tax Act, 1961 (“IT Act”) to
abolish the DDT regime. Accordingly, any dividend distribution by a domestic company is subject to tax in the hands of
the investor at the applicable rate. Additionally, the Company is required to withhold tax on such dividends distributed at
the applicable rate.

Investors are advised to consult their own tax advisors and to carefully consider the potential tax consequences of owning,
investing or trading in the Equity Shares. There is no certainty on the impact that the Finance Act may have on our business
and operations or on the industry in which we operate. Uncertainty in the applicability, interpretation or implementation of
any amendment to, or change in, governing law, regulation or policy, including by reason of an absence, or a limited body,
of administrative or judicial precedent may be time consuming as well as costly for us to resolve and may affect the viability
of our current business or restrict our ability to grow our business in the future.

We cannot predict whether any new tax laws or regulations impacting our services will be enacted, what the nature and
impact of the specific terms of any such laws or regulations will be or whether if at all, any laws or regulations would have
an adverse effect on our business. Further, any adverse order passed by the appellate authorities/ tribunals/ courts would
have an effect on our profitability. In addition, we are subject to tax related inquiries and claims.
